sources.originalTitle: Meet The Guy Who Solved Growing Apps (Hunter Isaacson Interview)
sources.summary: Hunter Isaacson walks through NGL's rise from six months of zero traction to 150M MAU, plus his earlier apps, Bags, and tactical advice on borrowing existing networks' distribution, selling users before tutorials, cheap regional weekly pricing, and spending a $20K/month budget on many small creative tests.

principles.text: Build on top of existing networks: swap the distribution mechanism of a proven behavior and improve the product.
principles.quote: find existing things that happen on other networks or other distribution mechanisms and just switch the distribution mechanism and improve the product to a certain degree

principles.text: Pick the biggest distribution graph; NGL beat predecessors by riding Instagram's link feature.
principles.quote: the reason NGL went as big as it did and has more downloads than all of those apps is because we use the biggest distribution graph of all which is the Instagram graph.

principles.text: Sell the end result in the call to action, not the app download.
principles.quote: it's way easier to get a download by saying get your own messages than saying, hey, download this app.

principles.text: Keep one flow, one funnel, and a single north-star metric; don't overcomplicate after going viral.
principles.quote: just how do you make it like one flow, one funnel, and don't over complicate it and just focus on like a northstar metric.

principles.text: Price weekly subscriptions as low-impulse buys scaled by regional GDP per capita; monetize a small share of a huge free user base.
principles.quote: It's priced differently depending on the region and depending on the GDP per capita of that country. So, it's always like a low impulse buy.

principles.text: With a ~$20K/month budget, run many small creative tests instead of betting on one, and pair them with an invite loop.
principles.quote: Don't spend all the money on like, you know, one specific creative. I would just test like a dozen of them.

sources.title: How Hunter Isaacson built NGL to 250M downloads: the consumer app playbook
sources.summary: Hunter Isaacson explains how he builds viral consumer apps (NGL, Wink, Bags): ship a bare-bones MVP, pick one northstar core action, seed with creators, bake sharing into the core flow, and use short slang brand names. He also covers finding ideas by applying proven formats to new channels.

principles.text: Start with a bare-bones MVP and get a few hundred or thousand users on quickly, even testing content before the app is live.
principles.quote: what's like my bare bones MVP version of this concept that is is good enough to solve the problem I'm trying to solve, but it's probably not optimized.

principles.text: Pick one northstar metric tied to a core action and orient every tradeoff decision around it.
principles.quote: if you have a northstar metric, it's kind of obvious what the decision would be. Um because you want to just increase that.

principles.text: Aim for over 90% of users completing the core action, through a single flow that everyone goes through.
principles.quote: when I say like a high percentage of people sharing the link and multiple replies, I mean over 90%.

principles.text: Use creators and TikTok/Instagram only to seed the app; once enough people download quickly, a built-in share loop takes over.
principles.quote: the purpose of the marketing was just to seed it, right? Just to get enough people to download it quickly.

principles.text: Put sharing or inviting inside the core action so growth does not rely only on the content that brought users in.
principles.quote: I do like to have some some kind of sharing or inviting in that in that core action

principles.text: Find ideas by taking proven formats and applying them to a new channel, rather than inventing from scratch.
principles.quote: Looking for like you know existing ideas that could work in a new channel. I feel like that's a great way to just find good ideas

sources.title: Hunter Isaacson: From failed apps to NGL and Bags, viral loops, taste, and failing faster
sources.originalTitle: From Losing $70,000 to $100M – Hunter Isaacson’s Journey
sources.summary: Hunter Isaacson recounts losing $70K on his first app, then shipping many apps until NGL hit 250M downloads. He explains viral loops, seeding with small creators then scaling winners with paid, why taste and EQ matter, and why he moved into consumer finance with Bags.

principles.text: Build a viral loop: users share something externally, friends see it and enter the same experience, then share it too.
principles.quote: I build these like loops where you just kind of For Bags, for example, the way we kind of got that company started is we had a growth loop about sharing your Bags link, right?

principles.text: Seed with small UGC creators paid on CPM, test content, then run the winning piece as paid in every market with variations.
principles.quote: I prefer like UGC type creators that like don't have a lot of followers that are like, you know, you can pay them on a CPM basis. And then I just like to test content.

principles.text: Seed, test, then run paid: put ad dollars behind content already proven to work organically.
principles.quote: So, it's like to me it's like seeding, testing, and then you run paid.

principles.text: Fail faster and ship many products; failures become your portfolio and eventually one works.
principles.quote: just fail faster. Because the faster you fail, the the faster you're going to succeed eventually.

principles.text: Get a minimum viable product live fast and iterate to see if it has legs.
principles.quote: I try to get a minimum viable product live quickly and then just iterate and just like move through it

principles.text: Consumer product success depends on taste and high EQ: understanding people lets you guide them through an experience.
principles.quote: I believe the most successful founders in consumer social specifically and and in in apps consumer apps have really high EQ.

sources.title: How Hunter Isaacson built NGL: simple, shareable apps that grow virally
sources.originalTitle: Who is this 24-Year Old Genius Behind Your Favorite Apps
sources.summary: Hunter Isaacson traces his path from failed first app Leader to Zoom University, Nine Count and NGL (100M+ downloads). Core lessons: design apps where each user brings the next, keep products radically simple, iterate on small tweaks, and treat failure unemotionally.

principles.text: Before building an app, ask how it grows organically: person A must bring person B.
principles.quote: if you're building an app make sure you figure out how how can person a bring person B and they bring person C and so on and so forth

principles.text: Frame every app as an exchange: define what you give the user and what you get from them.
principles.quote: what am I giving what am I getting and that's really important it's something think people don't really talk about enough is is that's really what this is it's it's a it's an exchange

principles.text: Build one simple thing that meets a specific demand; don't keep adding features once it works.
principles.quote: build something that just meets this specific demand and focus on that and don't over complicate it

principles.text: Make the app a funnel to share, so growth continues as long as people keep sharing it.
principles.quote: if the whole app is just about sharing then as long as somebody shares the app it's going to keep growing

principles.text: Small, measured tweaks turned a dud into a hit: test a change, keep wins, roll back losses.
principles.quote: making a change looking at the numbers and being like okay that was a good change let's do another one oh that was a bad change roll it back

principles.text: Go cross-platform: Android drove NGL's downloads worldwide while iPhone drove revenue.
principles.quote: Android gave us the downloads iPhone gave us the revenue

sources.title: How Hunter Isaacson built NGL and Bags: social app psychology, TikTok growth, niche communities
sources.originalTitle: How I Built a Social App That Made $2M in a Year | NGL Founder Story
sources.summary: Hunter Isaacson explains why social apps sell a feeling, how he goes from idea to Figma to devs to TikTok UGC testing, and why he's bullish on apps for niche internet communities. He also covers monetization (weekly subscriptions, fee sharing), the skill-tree approach to co-founders, and why you must exhaust every channel before quitting.

principles.text: Social apps sell a feeling, so the job is engineering the right emotional response, not shipping a utility.
principles.quote: with social apps, you're essentially selling air, right? You're you're selling a feeling.

principles.text: Social products must be shareable by design; shareability is the top thing to optimize for.
principles.quote: inherently it has to be sharable. I I think for a social app for social specifically yes it has to be sharable. Um that's like the most important thing that I focus on.

principles.text: Don't quit an app idea until you've exhausted every channel and activated everyone; most people quit too early.
principles.quote: most people want to quit and they have yet to actually exhaust every option and try every channel and get all everyone activated.

principles.text: Find the winning TikTok UGC format first, then turn it into ads and variations on fresh accounts.
principles.quote: test formats. Um, and then once you get a winning format, you just use that as an ad or you cut it and you create variations and you run them on on fresh accounts.

principles.text: Design the core loop and onboarding first, then have devs flag complexity so you can cut scope.
principles.quote: A lot of the times my devs just tell me like that's going to take us like you know a week. Do you really want to do that? I'm like no I don't obviously. So a lot of like prioritization.

principles.text: Best way to start: find behavior already on the internet in a niche community, optimize it, add a paywall.
principles.quote: just find behavior that already exists on the internet and then optimize that behavior and stick a a payw wall at some point in the flow.

sources.title: How Hunter Isaacson built NGL to 100M+ downloads: ship fast, build tools, talk like your users
sources.originalTitle: Meet the Rich 24/yo GENIUS Making Your Favorite Apps
sources.summary: Hunter Isaacson explains how he built NGL, an anonymous-message tool on top of Instagram, from about $10k to 100M+ downloads. He covers shipping fast, simple first-session funnels, riding another platform's graph, user-voice copy, and treating early failures as a portfolio.

principles.text: Speed wins: ship a bare-bones product fast and iterate; fast-shipping teams beat slower ones.
principles.quote: teams that ship fast win that's it it's super simple the faster you ship the faster you win

principles.text: Build tools that plug into existing behavior rather than new social networks.
principles.quote: if you want to build good products build tools not networks build tools that's what NGL is it's a tool

principles.text: Win the first session: clear expectation, one simple action, obvious reward, reaching the aha moment in about 60 seconds.
principles.quote: with any product you need a clear expectation a simple action and an obvious reward

principles.text: Piggyback on a giant platform by making an existing feature meaningfully better, then market it distinctively.
principles.quote: you find a way to make an existing product better and then you Market it in a unique way way and that's how you can do well on apps

principles.text: Write copy and run brand accounts in your audience's own slang and tone, memes and humor included.
principles.quote: talk like your user talks be memeable be funny

principles.text: Make users feel part of a movement by engaging, DMing and celebrating them publicly.
principles.quote: if you want to be successful in building Trends you have to make people feel that they're a part of a really big movement and you do that by you really engaging with them

sources.title: How Hunter J. Isaacson got NGL to 250M organic downloads with a friend-graph viral loop
sources.originalTitle: The 25-Year-Old App Designer Who Got 250 Million Downloads
sources.summary: Hunter J. Isaacson, a designer turned serial app founder, explains how NGL hit 250M downloads with zero paid marketing. He covers proving a viral loop in a small friend graph, one-step onboarding, one-action screens, GDP-based pricing, and equity structure.

principles.text: Prove the viral loop in one small friend graph first, then it scales globally.
principles.quote: prove the product by seeing if these people use it and then it spreads to everybody in their school. And if you can prove that once in a small scale it'll work globally basically.

principles.text: Design the first exposure as a friend's post, so social proof comes built in.
principles.quote: your first experience with NGL is seeing your friend post it, right? That's always your first experience.

principles.text: Cut onboarding to a single step to get users into the product fast.
principles.quote: our onboarding was one step. Um, which was literally just um type your Instagram username. No login, no authentication, no phone number, nothing.

principles.text: Give every screen one obvious central action, and polish it so it draws the eye.
principles.quote: I like to keep every page with like one central action because I think that people are easily distracted especially young people.

principles.text: Use a pay-or-share gate to turn free users into organic installs.
principles.quote: you can buy them for 99 cents or you can share on Snapchat and that feature just got us so many organic downloads.

principles.text: Localize pricing by country GDP so you do not price out parts of the world.
principles.quote: the pricing is different depending on the GDP of the country.

sources.title: How Hunter Isaacson built NGL and Bags: viral loops, session one, and launching before the product exists
sources.originalTitle: He Built Apps with 300M+ Downloads… Then Unlocked a Hidden Reality They Don’t Want You to Know About
sources.summary: Hunter Isaacson, co-founder of NGL and Bags (300M+ downloads across his apps), explains how he designs viral loops, onboarding and first-session experiences. He also covers launching with just the loop, spotting existing behavior to build on, and designing a lifestyle first. The back half drifts into worldview talk (humanoid robots, ancient tech, consciousness).

principles.text: Build the viral loop on social proof: users find the app via a friend's post, which signals it is safe, then onboarding takes seconds.
principles.quote: You already have that stamp of approval, then you go into the app, the onboarding is, you know, one, two steps, like nothing.

principles.text: Deliver the aha moment first, then ask for the share, in a way that fits the context (story, text to a friend).
principles.quote: you have to first deliver on the aha moment that just makes everything make sense to people and then you have to ask for sharing

principles.text: Launch with only the viral loop. Bags started with shareable links before the wallets even existed.
principles.quote: We didn't even have the wallets yet. We just had the the links. We started there.

principles.text: Optimize for session one over day-N retention: get users to do something valuable in the first session.
principles.quote: it's actually more about like the sessions. It's more about like can we get someone to do something in the first session?

principles.text: Design for conversion, not aesthetics. A/B test everything, even if the winning button is not the prettiest one.
principles.quote: it's not about making an art project, right? With these companies, it's about solving a problem

principles.text: Validate ideas by finding existing but unoptimized behavior on the internet or other apps, then package it better.
principles.quote: I'm looking for behavior that already exists, right?

sources.title: How Hunter Isaacson built NGL: viral loops, UGC seeding and bootstrapping consumer apps
sources.originalTitle: How he Built a $50M App Empire at 25 (Without Funding)
sources.summary: Hunter J. Isaacson explains how he went from failed apps to co-founding NGL (150M MAU) with about $5,000 and no venture funding. He covers picking ideas by psychological driver, designing viral loops where users market for you, using UGC only to seed the first users, monetizing without breaking the core promise, and why he avoided raising.

principles.text: Don't build features first. Find the drop-off point in the numbers, since a small tweak usually beats a new feature set.
principles.quote: I really learned to like not build first, but first like like first kind of figure out where is that that drop-off point? Where is that problem at?

principles.text: UGC only seeds the first few thousand users. A viral loop must carry the rest, otherwise you keep re-buying users.
principles.quote: It was only about like, can I get a thousand to ten thousand off of UGC, and then enough people will fall into the loop, and then they'll share it, and then more people come, right?

principles.text: Design the loop so sharing is a high-signal social endorsement that doesn't make the sharer look lame.
principles.quote: you want a viral loop that doesn't make you look lame, right? It makes you look socially acceptable.

principles.text: Make the new user's first action the one their friend benefits from, so they immediately want to be the next link in the chain.
principles.quote: your first experience with NGL was actually as the sender, not the receiver. So your first experience was seeing your friend post the link and you sending them the message.

principles.text: Only build ideas tied to a strong psychological driver; if you can't explain why user A would bring user B, skip it.
principles.quote: if I can't crack the like where it fits on the the Maslow's hierarchy of needs, then I won't build it, right?

principles.text: Find existing user behavior that is poorly optimized, then ship a noticeable product and brand improvement in an uncontested channel.
principles.quote: Find something that people are already doing that's not optimized and then try to optimize it with a faster flow and a better experience.

sources.title: Hunter Isaacson on not competing with your past self and building Bags after NGL
sources.originalTitle: He made $50 million but says money doesn't matter
sources.summary: Hunter Isaacson, founder of NGL and Bags, talks about moving from a viral social app to a crypto banking app. He covers bias to action, not repeating your first win, building what you personally need, and treating each exit as the next round. Much of the rest is spiritual and futurist speculation.

principles.text: Don't try to repeat your first win. You are no longer the underdog, so pick a different problem.
principles.quote: you already did that you were the underdog and you have that underdog story, but you're no longer the underdog.

principles.text: Just start building, and learn by failing. Bias to action beats waiting to feel qualified.
principles.quote: I was like 17 18 when I built my first company. I was just like I'm just going to do this like like what who cares? I'm just going to learn.

principles.text: Build the product you personally need. Your own fear of being debanked produced a bank.
principles.quote: I built this company selfishly like I built it for myself because I was worried that some of the ideas that I had. I would just be debanked

principles.text: Building in crypto takes years of hard infrastructure work, unlike investing, which takes minutes.
principles.quote: building in crypto requires years. Investing in crypto requires minutes, right?

principles.text: Cyclical markets change, so build the product to support whatever the asset class becomes.
principles.quote: we know crypto is cyclical and we know that the asset class is always changing. So whatever it ends up being, we're going to support everything.

principles.text: Treat each win as passing Go in Monopoly. Collect it and play the next round; the money does not change the work.
principles.quote: Okay, cool. I passed go. I got my couple million bucks. Now, let's go to the next round.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hunter Isaacson walks through NGL's rise from six months of zero traction to 150M MAU, plus his earlier apps, Bags, and tactical advice on borrowing existing networks' distribution, selling users before tutorials, cheap regional weekly pricing, and spending a $20K/month budget on many small creative tests.

chunks.heading: Background and track record
chunks.text:
- Hunter's first app, a social graph built around friends hanging out, took 2.5 years (started 2017) and never shipped. It died in TestFlight and was sunset in 2020. His takeaway: "I just loved the process of designing it so much that I realized that like this is what I should be doing with my life."
- Before NGL he had 70+ million downloads across other apps. These included Zoom University, a double-dating app for college kids, and Wink.
- Other apps he built:
  - A quotes, meditation and sleep-sounds app.
  - PopStream, a creator "meet and greet" app that was sunset.
  - A voice-chat mini-games app.
  - Bags, a crypto app.
- Wink let users swipe Tinder-style and added matches on Snapchat. It reached 70 million downloads.
- The mini-games app had close to an hour of average time spent per user, among the highest he has seen.
- NGL today has 150 million monthly active users and is a multi-8-figure-a-year business. That is far more than he expected.
- What he says makes someone good at viral consumer apps is understanding how people behave in groups: what a person feels when they see a screen, and how that emotion drives the action you ask for.

chunks.heading: How NGL went from zero to viral
chunks.text:
- Instagram opened link stickers to everyone at the end of October 2021 (before, you needed 10,000 followers). Hunter and friends got on a Zoom call on Halloween and decided to build an anonymous messaging app on top of Instagram. They built it in about a month.
- Then came 6 months of nobody using it. He assumed everyone saw the opportunity, and no one cloned NGL until after it went viral.
- What he tried during those 6 months:
  - Redesigned the app, then came up with the NGL name and the ngl.link domain.
  - Spent small amounts on influencers ("$100 here, $100 there") to post story links, plus TikToks.
- About 4 months in, a paid influencer activated a school on the other side of the world. It spread locally but not to other countries.
- He diagnosed it as a lower-income country, so they built Android quickly (May 2022). After a new marketing round, one TikTok went viral and took over the world within a week.
  - It showed a girl reading a controversial NGL message ("I was with your boyfriend last night") and trying to work out who sent it.
  - It got about 1 million views quickly and activated the first 1,000 users in one day.
  - The team tested many message texts and always tied them back to "you can get messages like this and maybe find out who sent it."

chunks.heading: Why NGL's viral loop holds up despite churn
chunks.text:
- Hunter says NGL is a "really tight viral loop." Many churned users came back because friends still post NGL links.
- In many countries it is effectively the link in bio for 17 to 19 year olds. A churned user sees a friend's link, sends a message, and wants their own.
- So it had churn but a very high redownload rate, which he credits for its lasting popularity.
- NGL looks very similar today to when it went viral. It has been optimized and made more fun, not loaded with feeds, extra tabs or complicated profile tools.
- He notes many anonymous apps over-complicated themselves after succeeding.
- NGL augments Instagram rather than competing with it. It opens inside Instagram as a lightweight interruption, and you can close it or go do it.

chunks.heading: NGL's funnel, copy and onboarding
chunks.text:
- Flow: copy link, then share. The share screen uses animated GIFs that show the steps (tap the sticker button, the link button, add the link, frame it).
- Posting through the app's flow auto-copies a branded asset with the user's profile picture.
- On the recipient side:
  - A dice button suggests what to say.
  - A persistent download button sits at the bottom.
  - After sending, the app prompts "get your own messages."
- He rates the "get your own messages" copy highly because it sells the result rather than the install: "it's way easier to get a download by saying get your own messages than saying, hey, download this app."
- Onboarding takes 15 to 20 seconds and drops the user straight onto the core screen.
- His lesson: make it one flow and one funnel, don't overcomplicate it, and focus on one north-star metric.
  - NGL's north star: how many people post the link and then post at least two replies.
- In the app, a message can show a hint (type of phone, rough location) or be replied to, which copies it onto the user's story.

chunks.heading: NGL monetization
chunks.text:
- Revenue is mostly weekly subscriptions.
- Prices vary by region and GDP per capita, always a low impulse buy of roughly $1 to $7.
- A very small percentage of downloads monetize. The product is primarily free.
- Paid users are power users who want more insights (who sent a message, who viewed their profile) or the "link games."
- Volume makes the small paid percentage add up to significant revenue.
- He thinks the model of a mass consumer social product with simple monetization, grown on the back of big networks, is still open.

chunks.heading: Frameworks for finding app ideas
chunks.text:
- The core pattern: take an existing behavior from another network or distribution channel, switch the distribution mechanism, and improve the product.
  - Anonymous Q&A had existed before (YOLO, Yik Yak, Formspring). NGL won by riding the Instagram graph, the biggest distribution graph.
- Pick the graph you target: Instagram, Snapchat, X, or Facebook for 45-year-old moms. "It doesn't really matter."
- Smaller or niche graphs are an opportunity, and he sees more of them emerging. He says you can also build a super viral experience on a big platform like Twitter and it will work.
- Design insight from Zoom University:
  - The waitlist hit about 40,000 people with a 7:1 girl-to-guy ratio, which is unheard of in dating.
  - Women do things when they're comfortable because they're with another woman.
  - Format: a group chat plus private chat, double opt-in on both sides, then a group chat if matched.
  - Zoom University had a few hundred thousand downloads and reached the top 10 of the social category.
- Cost lesson from PopStream: influencer pricing was too high (a top influencer posting a link cost about $20,000), so the economics didn't work.

chunks.heading: Share menu and Safari extension plays
chunks.text:
- He advised a video-saving app called Fade, which blew up and went close to number one. Users tap share, tap more, scroll to Fade, and it saves videos that would otherwise be deleted from TikTok.
- The share-menu or recipe-app playbook works if users understand the value. A multi-step setup tutorial is fine then. It worked for NGL because users had already seen friends get messages.
- Rule: sell the user effectively before the tutorial, make the tutorial simple, and measure drop-off at each step.
- He also advises a company building a Safari extension (credit card recommendations at checkout). It works once you get past user education, and works best when the app runs in the background.
  - Install is five to six steps, so the user must already be fully sold before the tutorial.
- He likes adding social elements to everything, such as invite screens and nudging users to share. Sharing an app is an endorsement from a friend, and he puts it in every product when it makes sense.

chunks.heading: Bags: product and revenue model
chunks.text:
- Bags is a crypto app aimed at solving token discovery. It shows influencers' buys in real time, with market cap and percent change, and a quick-buy button.
- Group chats have trading built in, unlike Telegram where you need a bot and typed commands.
- The wallet is designed like a credit card rather than a typical wallet. You can send by username and deposit with Apple Pay (via Moonpay) or crypto.
- Revenue:
  - A 1% fee on transactions, with most of the fee passed back to the friend who invited you. Someone who posts a token in a group chat also earns some commission when others buy it.
  - A token launchpad with a 1% royalty on every trade, not only on the LP transaction. His example: $2 million of volume yields $20,000.
- On crypto games: he thinks a successful one will happen but it's a whole other beast.
  - Teams often focus on money over the player experience and social graph.
  - Game user acquisition is very competitive and dominated by paid ads, so games are a hard place for a small team to start.

chunks.heading: Scaling an app from $10K MRR with a $10K to $20K budget
chunks.text:
- Put a good amount of the money into UGC with influencers or ads, run as experiments.
- Track which cohort came from which ad or TikTok, and keep adapting formats.
- Run many small tests, such as a dozen creatives, rather than putting everything into one.
- Focus on product-led growth: use the ads to bring people in, then get them to invite a friend immediately.
- If a percentage of users bring someone else, your effective CPI drops considerably.
- Find the best hook to get someone in, then get a percentage to share. Once an ad format works and the invite loop works, scale the content up and look for other distribution channels.
- Spend primarily on tests until you hit a format that works. That is where "the flywheel really kicks off."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hunter Isaacson explains how he builds viral consumer apps (NGL, Wink, Bags): ship a bare-bones MVP, pick one northstar core action, seed with creators, bake sharing into the core flow, and use short slang brand names. He also covers finding ideas by applying proven formats to new channels.

chunks.heading: Start with a simple v1, not a polished product
chunks.text:
Hunter's playbook for a $1M/month consumer app begins with the bare-bones MVP.
- He defines the V1 feature set as "good enough to solve the problem" but "probably not optimized" and "rough on the edges."
- He gets a few hundred to a few thousand users on quickly.
- He tests content on TikTok or Instagram Reels before the app is live, even at pre-order stage. The question is whether the formats the app is premised on actually get a response.
- He designs every app himself in Figma, branding included (about a dozen apps solo). He started in PowerPoint, then Photoshop, then Sketch, then Figma.

chunks.heading: Pick one North Star metric and a single core action
chunks.text:
Hunter wants one metric that "matters more than the other ones," because it makes tradeoff decisions obvious.
- **Wink** (make-new-friends swiping app): percentage of users who get a match on day one. He used the matching algorithm to pair heavy swipers with new users.
- **NGL:** percentage of users who share the link and share a few replies. Sharing was a four-step process with a tutorial. Seeing friends get replies made viewers more willing to send messages.
- **Bags** (crypto app): how many new users fund their account and make one trade on day one.
- If a decision works against the North Star, "it's just not the right decision."
- He wants over 90% of users completing the core action, with everyone going through one identical flow. Branching journeys make results hard to read.

chunks.heading: Build sharing or inviting into the core action
chunks.text:
- Once the core action is proven, he builds sharing or inviting into it so growth isn't fully reliant on the TikTok video or ad that brought the user.
- Example: if 1,000 users drop in and 50% share, that is 500 more people reached, which raises the K factor.
- Hard invite gates can work. He cites Lapse (a viral photo app) requiring roughly three to five friend invites: many users hit the wall, but those who pass are extremely valuable.
- On NGL, almost every user went through the share step.
- Bags loops: log in with Twitter, claim a Bags link, share it, and invited users are credited on a leaderboard. Top Solana-ecosystem people appeared on it. The loops grew hype and followers to 100,000 on Twitter before the product was fully built out.
- For single-player apps (the Hallow example), he says to nail the single-player daily habit first. Social and multiplayer are then a growth lever, along with gating monetization behind a share or offering a discount for inviting friends and family.

chunks.heading: Seed with creators, then let the loop take over
chunks.text:
- Marketing exists to "seed" the app: get enough people to download in a tight window so the growth loop activates.
- NGL spent less than $10,000 on marketing in total to reach a quarter billion downloads. He paid roughly $50 to $100 here and there for influencers to post the link on their story.
- For Wink he paid TikTokers to make videos.
- After the core action is proven, he applies more pressure: new audiences, niches, creators in other countries and time zones.
- His principle is not to pay a lot. Test small, build things that work at small scale, and "all you really need is that one viral video." Paid or free depends on creator and agency relationships, with no standard answer.

chunks.heading: Old ideas in new channels
chunks.text:
- NGL was not a new idea (he names Ask.fm and Yik Yak). It launched when Instagram opened link stickers to everyone in October 2021, previously requiring 10,000 followers. He and friends were building within days and shipped in a few weeks.
- It then took about six months to seed. He also had to train users to tap the link sticker, paste, and position it.
- His takeaway: don't reinvent the wheel. Look for a proven idea plus a new distribution channel, and for something "not optimized on this platform."
- He encourages thinking in frameworks over ideas: "NGL for X, Cali for X, Locket for X, Pangu for X."
- Examples he praises: Cal AI (simple tool, packaged with an onboarding funnel that makes it seem more valuable than it is), Locket (first to make the iPhone widget social), Pangu (AI-powered virtual pets).
- He points to unexploited Apple surfaces: live activities and lock screen widgets.
- Apple's yearly iOS releases often hand builders new real estate.

chunks.heading: Brand and name: short, slang, on the nose
chunks.text:
- Names like NGL ("not going to lie"), Wink and Bags are short and obvious about what the app is. He says complicated names confuse people.
- Using a community's slang as the name sets a young, comfortable, colloquial tone. He carries that language into popups and in-app copy, so the app feels like it understands the user.
- He notes it was surprising nobody had built a crypto app called Bags.
- He stresses an authentic, memeable, relatable voice. NGL has about 2 million Instagram followers and runs meme formats and funny messages. Bags has over 100,000 Twitter followers, posts daily, and has an intern who keeps it active. He says it increases affinity, trust and sharing.

chunks.heading: Why young builders should do consumer
chunks.text:
- He advises people in their teens, 20s and college years to take many swings, and recommends consumer mobile apps over B2B or SaaS.
- Reasons: you learn human psychology, how to build products people love and how to go viral, and you can reach the whole world. It's about building and marketing rather than contracts.
- He says AI tools are getting good enough that you will soon not need a technical cofounder, though "we're not fully there yet."
- He's bullish on consumer crypto going mainstream with regulation, and on AR glasses driven by the phone's compute.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hunter Isaacson recounts losing $70K on his first app, then shipping many apps until NGL hit 250M downloads. He explains viral loops, seeding with small creators then scaling winners with paid, why taste and EQ matter, and why he moved into consumer finance with Bags.

chunks.heading: Path into apps and the early failures
chunks.text:
- Hunter started building apps at 17-18, near the end of high school. His first app was a "Gen Z Foursquare": go to locations, earn points, rank on leaderboards.
- It took about 2.5 years of learning and failing. He spent about $70,000 on outsourced developers in India and says it was "gone". He also raised $150,000 at age 19.
- COVID lockdowns killed the app. He took it as a sign: "this is not my billion-dollar app, but I really love building apps."
- Within 6-8 weeks he built Zoom University as a designer with friends. It was a live college double-date video app that matched two friends with two friends. It hit top 10 in social, got a few hundred thousand downloads, and ran about a 7:1 girl-to-guy ratio.
- He says it "proved a point": after 2.5 years of failing, he could do it.
- He was recruited at 21 by a Musical.ly co-founder and former president, and worked there for just under 2 years. They built about half a dozen apps, including Wink, which reached roughly 50-60 million downloads and #1 in the App Store.
- He then built NGL, which became the largest anonymous social app and freed him from his 9-to-5.

chunks.heading: Failing fast and persistence
chunks.text:
- Hunter's core advice is "fail faster." He says the faster you fail, the faster you succeed. He tells people to seek rejection and failure as the goal, throw things at the wall, tweak, and learn.
- In 2021 he built and shipped 5-6 apps. The last one became NGL. His mindset was "I'm going to ship this and if it fails, I don't care." A failed app goes on the portfolio site: "failure is just your portfolio."
- It took 5 years from starting to becoming a millionaire.
- He says the people who win are the ones who never quit. He has seen very smart people stop shipping just before one worked, and says he has never seen a smart, relentless person fail to succeed.
- After meeting many founders, he concluded most are "just dudes" who didn't quit. Seeing friends succeed made it feel possible.
- When you feel like giving up, he says, that is when to double down.
- He says to love the process: "you have to enjoy the journey," and chasing the next goal leads to a dopamine treadmill.

chunks.heading: Why apps, and how to build one
chunks.text:
- He calls apps "the best business in the world" and the "greatest creative expression," since a product can reach billions of people. He admits the learning curve is steep and says consumer social is the hardest category for product-market fit: "you're selling a feeling."
- His build process: start with an idea, design it himself, have stronger engineers build it, get a minimum viable product live fast, then iterate and change things.
- NGL was built in about 3 weeks. Nobody used it for about 6 months while he tried to seed a high-school friend graph. He was convinced it would work.
- One TikTok hit a million views. In the first week of June, downloads went from about 1,000 in a day to 1.5 million in a day, then about 90,000 downloads an hour. At the time he earned $100K a year at his job, and the app was making that in a day.
- He expected a ceiling of 10 million downloads. NGL passed 250 million, with 10-20 million concurrent users at times, on Firebase. Most engineers say Firebase can't scale. Because the stack was simple, he knew where failures would occur, and the app had only small outages of up to an hour.
- He predicts a "golden age of apps" when a new compute platform (glasses, contacts) coincides with good AI tools that let people build with their voice.
- On tools, he says Cursor is very good and most of his engineers use it.

chunks.heading: Viral loops and influencer marketing
chunks.text:
- Hunter builds "organic virality" through viral loops. He describes it as: you share something externally, a friend sees it and enters the same experience, and they share it because you did.
- For Bags, the loop was sharing your Bags link, which works like your wallet address and profile link. Users logged in with Twitter, generated a link, and shared it immediately. This brought in hundreds of thousands of people and "growth hacked" the first couple of months.
- His influencer playbook is seeding, testing, then paid:
  - Seed so the first ~1,000 people download or interact, then use a viral mechanic to get them to share and invite friends.
  - He prefers smaller accounts and UGC-type creators with few followers, paid on a CPM basis.
  - Test content, and once a TikTok wins, run it as an ad in every market. Translate it, make variations such as changing the sound, and push hard.
- He says using organic virality as proof of concept before spending on ads is "a great strategy."
- For Bags, he said influencer work was planned and that growth was only now being turned on after a long building phase.

chunks.heading: Bags and choosing consumer finance
chunks.text:
- Hunter started Bags' company in summer 2023, expecting crypto to come back. He wanted to be live when it did, because being on chain with many eyeballs coming in generates volume.
- He chose consumer finance for a longer runway, since he said consumer social gets harder to stay tapped into as you age. He wanted something he could run for 5 years and into his 30s.
- He didn't want to compete with himself on downloads after NGL. Instead of chasing a quarter-billion users, he aimed for average revenue per user: maybe 5 million downloads and a very successful fintech business.
- NGL monetizes a small percentage of users, though it makes eight figures a year.
- Bags earns from a small transaction fee, split with affiliates. If someone joins through your link, you get half their fees. If someone copies your trade, you also earn a share. Some users have made tens of thousands of dollars this way.
- He says the hardest part has been the technical moat: finance, trading, landing transactions, and complicated data.

chunks.heading: Hiring, team and autonomy
chunks.text:
- His engineers are all in Europe, including his CTO, front end, and back end, in places like Portugal, Austria, Poland and Spain. He wanted to hire in Miami but couldn't find enough devs with crypto experience.
- Crypto development is hard because there is little documentation and no forums of people helping.
- He found engineers through community members who reached out, recruiters, and various sites. His head of ops has interviewed about 50 engineers.
- His approach: hire smart people, give them autonomy, and trust the right people. Each co-founder owns a lane, such as his CTO owning engineering. He owns design and sets the flow, look and vibe, then adjusts to what engineering and marketing do.
- He prefers co-founders over going solo: "I would rather give away half the business to someone who's worth it." He says solo is lonely and he wants "to win with people."
- He tests ideas by asking friends to "roast this" with no emotion, and avoids yes-men.
- He sees himself moving from doing everything to operating, and says a founder is "never above the work." He joined his engineers for an all-nighter in Singapore right after about 30 hours of travel.

chunks.heading: Taste, EQ and finding your lane
chunks.text:
- Hunter's edge is design and taste, built from Minecraft building, LEGO, art and Photoshop. He designed his first app in Photoshop.
- He thinks taste will be the most important skill as AI improves, and that AI getting real taste will take a long time.
- Much of his work is psychology: for example, making a button big, green and pulsing so users tap it. He aims to move people through an experience so "they don't even think," manage the cognitive load of a screen, and direct the eyes.
- He learned this from iterating on apps and making and testing hypotheses, not from books.
- He argues the best consumer app founders have high EQ because they understand people.
- Universal principle: make users feel comfortable and trust you. People only share things they don't think are lame, so anything that makes them cringe or feel confused kills sharing. Keep the product simple so they know what to do.
- He advises specializing: pick one skill (design, engineering, marketing, growth, editing) and get very good, then provide value to others. That builds a network and a bench of complementary co-founders. He cites Brian Chesky and Evan Spiegel as "design CEOs" who inspired him to own the design lane.
- When reaching out to high-value people, offer value first rather than asking for something.

chunks.heading: Habits, health and mindset
chunks.text:
- He had no balance last year, and now travels with his team (Singapore, Thailand, Bali, Bahamas, Portugal, Colombia) while staying productive.
- His morning routine: no phone on waking (it sits on the floor away from the bed), grounding outside, stretching, push-ups, reading a chapter, music, gratitude and manifestation writing, a healthy breakfast and supplements. Then he sits down for lock-in work.
- He recommends 50-100 push-ups a day, and says training is practice at showing up daily for slow rewards.
- Health: he started biohacking at about 23 after a doctor friend told him he'd be very healthy in 20 years. He tests blood levels and takes supplements, and cut processed foods, artificial dyes and "natural flavors." He says eating a clean, balanced meal lets him focus for about 6 hours afterward.
- He advises young people to take responsibility and ownership of a product or mission, because men need a mission. Try a handful of things over several years, find your purpose, then go all in.
- He says chase passion that can also make money, and that when you're young, "pay now or pay later." Surround yourself with high-value, hard-working people.
- He believes in manifestation and the law of attraction, treating it as focus plus hard work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hunter Isaacson traces his path from failed first app Leader to Zoom University, Nine Count and NGL (100M+ downloads). Core lessons: design apps where each user brings the next, keep products radically simple, iterate on small tweaks, and treat failure unemotionally.

chunks.heading: Hunter's first apps: Leader and the lessons from failing young
chunks.text:
- Hunter's first app, Leader, was a "gen Z Foursquare." He built it at 17-18, convinced it would make him a billionaire before 22.
- It took about 2.5 years and failed. He calls it "a 2 and a half year lesson on everything that I shouldn't have done in business."
- His main lesson was never to outsource development. He should also have gone to people who knew how to build instead of hiding from experts out of imposter syndrome.
- He over-obsessed on pixel-perfect design and the wrong things, which made the app complicated and hard to build.
- He argues for emotional detachment in a first business: "business is really just like shoveling [expletive] and failing." If it fails, "who cares," because once you've succeeded once, you can have 10-30 failures in your portfolio.
- He applied to YC (once or twice) and other accelerators and was rejected everywhere. His view is that accelerators are good to get into but "not going to make or break it."
- His advice to early-stage founders: "just go fail." Fall on your face, and don't worry about what your high-school friends think.

chunks.heading: Zoom University: a simple, social product built at the right moment
chunks.text:
- Zoom University was a double-dating app for college students, launched during COVID. The idea came from a friend, Daniel, and Hunter joined as designer. They shipped the app within about 24 hours of agreeing to work together.
- Why college students: the younger you skew, the more close friends each user has. Anything meant to spread organically and virally should target the people with the most social connections (college, high school, middle school).
- Double dating worked because girls are more comfortable going out with a friend. The app ended up with a 7-to-1 girl-to-guy ratio.
- Timing helped: parties disappeared and college kids wanted to meet each other.
- It made little money but went viral and reached the top 10 of the App Store. He calls it a "moderate W" after the big L of Leader, and says it proved to him this was possible.
- The contrast between Leader and Zoom U taught him his core lesson: build something simple that meets one specific demand. Leader was complicated and failed; Zoom U was a very simple product that went viral.

chunks.heading: Consulting for big brands and building at Nine Count
chunks.text:
- After Zoom U, Hunter did consulting for Fortune 500 brands, helping them reach younger audiences. He found it frustrating because he couldn't change anything (fonts, colors, advice) without layers of marketing approval. It convinced him he wanted to own his own thing and not be "a small cog in a big machine."
- He then joined Nine Count, a consumer social holding company led by Alex Hoffman, former president of Musical.ly (acquired by ByteDance for about $1B). Alex became his first mentor.
- He deliberately chose to be a designer/product person for a while, citing Evan Spiegel and Brian Chesky as "design CEOs."
- At Nine Count he designed 10 apps and shipped 5. The first focus was Wink, which became the largest Snapchat friend-finder. Wink and others got free organic downloads from Snapchat, which taught him the importance of a constant influx of new users.
- He describes this period as "paying my dues," working with experts and tens of millions of VC dollars behind the team.
- His favorite app there was a voice-chat game app: match with a stranger, play hyper-casual games, then swap Snapchats. It had some of the best foundational metrics he has ever seen but was shut down by Apple for violating terms.

chunks.heading: How to build a viral app: the exchange and the share loop
chunks.text:
- Start with the user journey. Ask what you get from the user (name, phone number, Instagram handle) and what you give them (dopamine, followers, a cool photo). He says: "It's an exchange."
- The sequence: concept and journey, heavy design work (Figma prototyping), front-end build (SwiftUI for iOS, or React Native for cross-platform), then App Store submission. He calls himself a front-end engineer who prefers to be the product lead running design, product and marketing, and says his product skills are stronger than his engineering skills.
- App Store rejections are usually mundane: a missing privacy policy or a missing restore-purchase button. Approval generally comes after one or two rejections.
- Growth rule: build something that can be shared organically. "Make sure you figure out how person A can bring person B and they bring person C." He says many people skip this step and "build products that don't work."
- His first question for any app, and the one he asks the founders he advises: "How does this grow organically?" If you aren't asking it, "you failed level one."
- He pushes back on features that nobody would share ("no one's going to share that, this is lame").
- App Store ranking is a "pure meritocracy": no cheat code, and you can't run ads to reach number one. Only about a hundred teams really compete at the top, and the business is built on failing over and over before something works.
- Staying viral is hard; most apps get 15 minutes, fail to monetize and raise at inflated valuations. Hunter designs apps so the entire app is a funnel to share, so growth continues as long as people keep sharing.

chunks.heading: NGL: building and growing the anonymous Q&A app
chunks.text:
- NGL was anonymous Q&A for Instagram stories. It was built with co-founder Isaiah and others on the day Instagram opened link stickers to everyone. The team assumed every team would do the same thing, so they built it in 3 weeks.
- Nobody copied them, and the app was a dud for about 4-6 months. Hunter says he knew it would work from first principles: it grows automatically through Instagram, the gossip is juicy, teens love anonymous apps, and it is a tool, not a platform.
- The company was built with $10,000, most of which went to a domain they never used. The rest paid influencers about $100-200 each.
- The hardest problem was the share flow. Users had to copy the link, copy the asset, open Instagram and place the link. NGL effectively trained 100M+ people to use links in stories.
- Small tweaks that turned it around:
  - Renamed from "ask.fun" to NGL.
  - Made the tutorial unskippable.
  - Tweaked button copy and added a disclaimer.
  - Added "100% anonymous and secure" text on the website, which made people willing to send crazier messages.
- He describes the method as making a change, checking the numbers, keeping good changes and rolling back bad ones, "for months and months."
- The app first popped off in New Zealand (April/May 2022, about 7,000 users, roughly $2K that month). They used that window to iterate, add monetization and test social post styles.
- It went viral about a week after they launched the Android app. His takeaway: "Android gave us the downloads, iPhone gave us the revenue." Viral in places like Tunisia, Romania, Puerto Rico, Asia, Europe and South America. He now builds everything cross-platform, and notes the Middle East/North Africa and Southeast Asia download new apps eagerly.

chunks.heading: NGL monetization and results
chunks.text:
- Monetization was copied from apps in the same space: a weekly subscription selling premium features. They built it in before going viral, during the New Zealand test.
- His view on copying: "everybody copies each other and they copy each other publicly... the playbook is in front of you."
- On scale: you don't need many paying users when it's a weekly subscription, because "a couple hundred people" quickly adds up.
- Numbers he gives: 150M+ downloads, about 60-70% of his total revenue from NGL, and roughly $40M total revenue across all the apps he has built. The company cash-flowed $1 million in its first viral month. His income went from about $100,000 a year to that amount per day.
- The app never fell off a cliff. Revenue went up and stayed. Partners now run day-to-day operations.
- He kept the app unchanged on purpose. Many apps ruin a good thing by piling on features (he cites Snapchat adding a feed, a map and shows). Everyone pitched him ways to turn NGL into something bigger, and he ignored them: "we're not building a social platform here, this is a tool, it's a social utility."
- When the app blew up, there was no celebration at first: press, copycats, competitors and lawsuits arrived at once. The celebrating came months later.

chunks.heading: Design principles: simplicity, magic moments and tolerating churn
chunks.text:
- Keep it simple: build something that just does what it's supposed to do, and don't bog it down with unnecessary features.
- Build for the one-time user. "Build this for one person is going to use it one time... make sure the app can survive if 90% of the people use it once." If you churn on day one, he's fine as long as he got something: either monetized you or got you to share.
- He believes that this philosophy leads to daily retention, because you end up optimizing the key moments.
- Deliver the "magic moment" in the first 60 seconds: get something from the user, give them the dopamine, then let them run. If they don't come back, fine; if they do, great.
- Apps that require constant attention don't last as long because there are too many alternatives. A tool that sits on top of a durable platform (Instagram) can last a decade.
- Use human nature: people share an app when it gives them a good feeling and makes them look cool, which he calls "a very fair exchange."
- Make the work fun: "if it's a little bit more fun... you're going to much more enjoy your time in the trenches."

chunks.heading: Bags app and where Hunter is going next
chunks.text:
- He is building Bags, which he describes as the Discord/Telegram replacement for financial messaging. Its core idea: "if you own an asset, you are now in a chat about that asset," starting with holder chats and Alpha-chat communities.
- He says it is a crypto/finance app where users never see the words crypto, NFT or web3. He loves the technology but dislikes the "web 3" packaging: "just give them a product that makes sense that you use the technology in the back end."
- Why fintech: the ceiling for NGL-type apps is limited and "you can't get into the billion dollar club" with them, while financial apps have more valuable data, users with more money and a different demographic. He wants "an arena where the ceiling is much higher."
- He is also working on other, unannounced products with several teams. They are social but not anonymous, built on the same thesis of sharing loops and flywheels: "I bring someone and they bring someone."
- He advises other founders and says several companies he works with have built number-one apps. He typically asks them why a feature exists and how it will grow.
- Outlook: he thinks the golden age of apps is ahead, driven by Gen Z and Gen Alpha gaining spending power and by AR glasses plus advanced generative AI in about five years. He plans to build everything he wants on the phone form factor before moving to AR/VR.
- His stated plan is to put his head down for the next four to five years, with the goal of becoming a multi-billionaire. His mindset: "the people that created everything in the world are no smarter than me." His father's advice: "Don't chase money, chase your passion, just make sure your passion can make money."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hunter Isaacson explains why social apps sell a feeling, how he goes from idea to Figma to devs to TikTok UGC testing, and why he's bullish on apps for niche internet communities. He also covers monetization (weekly subscriptions, fee sharing), the skill-tree approach to co-founders, and why you must exhaust every channel before quitting.

chunks.heading: Social apps are selling a feeling, so psychology comes first
chunks.text:
- Hunter started at 18 with an app idea he thought would take six months and make him a billionaire by 21. He then spent two and a half years failing.
- His view: "with social apps, you're essentially selling air... you're selling a feeling." It is not SaaS or fintech. The job is to engineer the right dopamine response so users enjoy the process more than they would a plain product or service.
- He frames social apps as selling belonging and a way to connect with other people, which is intangible.
- For social specifically, the app has to be shareable. That is the most important thing he focuses on.
- He built apps in the LA consumer scene of 2020-2021, when it was small and everyone knew each other. His co-founder on Bags was met in a Discord server called Gen Z Mafia during COVID.

chunks.heading: Path to NGL: Leader, Zoom University, then the anonymous messaging hit
chunks.text:
- **Leader (first app, age 18):** "Foursquare for Gen Z." Users went to locations, earned points, got ranked on leaderboards with friends and made content. COVID killed it. He raised $150,000 at about 19 and burned through it, but learned a lot.
- **Zoom University:** built about 6 weeks after Leader failed, with a couple of friends. College kids were bored and lonely during COVID, and "Zoom University" was already a meme, which gave it ready-made branding. They seeded Facebook groups and pushed content. The first version ran on Zoom meeting links, then became an app with a couple hundred thousand downloads. It gave him the confidence that this was possible.
- **NGL:** Instagram had just launched link sharing for every user (previously you needed 10,000 followers). Within a call with friends they decided to build anonymous messaging for Instagram. Earlier apps like Sarahah and Yolo had done well on Snapchat, so they replicated the model on a bigger channel.
- NGL took about six months from launch to going viral. For those six months it was "basically crickets."
- He believed it would work because it needed enough initial density, clusters of friends all sharing at the same time. Once that happened it went super viral.

chunks.heading: Validating an app idea: exhaust every option before quitting
chunks.text:
- Hunter says he has no formal validation process.
- He watches core metrics: everyone getting through onboarding, decent retention, minimized churn (at least early on), and some decent monetization.
- His main warning: people give up on an app idea before reaching those numbers. "You just need to exhaust all your options."
- Only move on if you have exhausted every option, tried every channel and gotten everyone activated and it still isn't working. Most people want to quit before doing that.
- He says the NGL "crickets" period shows why: the idea needed critical density, not a different product.

chunks.heading: His process from idea to App Store, and the first-thousand-users push
chunks.text:
1. **Ideation:** think through the idea, sometimes a write-up, sometimes a "word salad" on the page. Identify the core experience and core loop, whether it is shareable, and the onboarding funnel.
2. **Design in Figma:** do branding and colors, and design onboarding first because he needs the data for accounts. Onboarding length depends on the app. Some are long funnels ending in a monetization event. NGL's is a few steps done in 15-20 seconds.
3. **Screen-by-screen design** of the whole app.
4. **Ask devs for feedback:** "Are there technical issues... Is this too complicated?" Devs often say a feature will take a week and ask if he really wants it. Often he does not, so it forces prioritization around the core app flow.
5. **Build and iterate** through multiple builds and TestFlights. He sends TestFlight screenshots with drawings on them so the team can fix problems.
6. **Submit to the App Store.**
7. After launch the goal is to "drop a thousand people into this" and see what they do.

chunks.heading: Organic marketing and TikTok as the app channel
chunks.text:
- Hunter says TikTok is currently the channel for promoting apps.
- He and friends ran the "fresh account strategy" on TikTok in 2019 and heavily in 2020, learning the algorithm's tricks years ago.
- His playbook: run TikTok UGC with agencies, creators and people he knows, and test formats. When a format wins, use it as an ad, cut variations and run them on fresh accounts.
- With Bags, the team first focused on a technical moat: a reliable, fast, performant trading app. The focus has now shifted to activation: more funded accounts and more people brought into the app.
- A related sign of the app-store view: he says getting to number one overall, which he has done multiple times in 150 countries, is "extremely difficult" and has no shortcuts.

chunks.heading: App Store as a meritocracy, and the 30% fee
chunks.text:
- Hunter calls the App Store a pure meritocracy: "There is no way of actually fudging the numbers." If an app is number one, it is because people are using it.
- Everyone builds with the same software, the same phone and the same tools, and whoever packages them best goes number one. He calls it a source of truth and "a window into pop culture."
- On Apple's 30% cut: he calls it "the mafia tax" and says he does not think it is fair, though it is fair that Apple takes something. He says every developer would agree.
- His critique of the Small Business Program (under $1 million a year, application required): it is not tiered like taxes. If you make $1,010,000 you drop from keeping about $850,000 of the first million to about $700,000, which he calls unfair.
- He thinks young developers entering apps will be turned off by having a "silent partner" that approves or disapproves everything they do.

chunks.heading: Monetization models: NGL weekly subscription and Bags fee share
chunks.text:
- **NGL:** a weekly subscription. A small percentage of its hundreds of millions of users convert. The premium version gives insights on who sends you messages (who, where, their deal) while still staying anonymous. It does not reveal names, mostly because they do not know them. In rare cases where they do know, they display it.
- **Bags:** takes a small fee per transaction on buys and sells (not on sending and receiving). It passes 50-75% of those fees back to users. Examples: if you share your Bags link, your friend signs up and trades, you earn his fees. If you buy a token, someone sees it on the For You page and buys it, you earn the fee.
- His aim is a structure where "the people benefit, not just the platform," giving back the majority of what the app earns.

chunks.heading: Why Bags: mobile-first crypto for Gen Z and Gen Alpha
chunks.text:
- Hunter has been in crypto since 2017, joining when Bitcoin was $1,000. His belief is that personal sovereignty and financial education matter for his generation, and financial literacy has been lackluster or non-existent.
- The thesis: put banking on crypto rails, make it social and fun, and build a bank for Gen Z and Gen Alpha. He wants to eventually support stocks, bonds and bank accounts.
- He chose mobile because he knows mobile better, and because crypto "has to go native mobile to really break out." Being in the App Store is a trust factor, especially for financial apps.
- Bags currently focuses on Solana and Solana memecoins because that is where the attention is. He wants a business he can work on for five-plus years: an "adult company" with a strong team, a strong tech stack and a moat.
- On memecoins: he sees them as monetizing attention and news cycles, and says "the internet is all betting on attention." He notes many people are tired of the current memecoin iteration, but each crypto cycle brings a new asset class (ICOs, then NFTs), and he says the asset class for this cycle is still unseen.
- He argues memecoins give the same effect as gambling, but simpler, for people who spend their time online.

chunks.heading: Gen Z behavior, building for the "seven sins," and finding niches
chunks.text:
- Gen Z cares a lot about belonging and community, and about impact in a social sense: "can I get views, can I get clout, can I get attention." He says they grew up in instability (the 2008 era, then COVID) and live in a "post-truth era," which makes them caring but sensitive.
- He says people respond to incentives, which explains the shift from degrees and 9-to-5s toward creators.
- On "build for the seven deadly sins": the most electrically charged emotions (greed, lust and so on) hook people into a product. He admits the trade-off: it makes money but is "probably not going to have good impact," and it relies on dark patterns.
- His advice on niches: he is very bullish on niche internet communities. Find behavior that already exists on the internet (subreddits, Facebook groups), build a product for it, and "stick a paywall at some point in the flow." He says such niche products can reach $100,000+ a month in MRR and are easy to target on TikTok.
- His example: the looksmaxxing community on TikTok, for which Blake Anderson built UMAX.
- On AI apps: he expects accuracy to keep improving ("wait three months, six months, a year") and says Cal AI works because photo-based logging is far easier than the boring input flow of MyFitnessPal.

chunks.heading: Team building and getting started as a young founder
chunks.text:
- **Three skills a consumer app needs:** engineering, product and growth. They can be one person or five. On NGL he was product, one co-founder was an engineer and another was growth marketing. On Bags he does product, co-founders do engineering, and they share growth.
- His advice to a 21-year-old: pick one skill (design, engineering or UGC/TikTok growth), get known for it in your circle, then find people to fill your "skill tree."
- **Hiring:** all his Bags engineers are in Europe, and he has had amazing experiences with European developers. He finds talent through networking, socials and heavy interviewing. His head of operations did about 60 interviews to build a catalog of available talent.
- Crypto hiring is hard: documentation is minimal, and it is hard to find someone who knows React Native, understands Solana and is Web3 native.
- **Mindset:** "everything in your life is your fault," good and bad. He treats total ownership as a process of asking how you contributed to something bad, rather than blaming others.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hunter Isaacson explains how he built NGL, an anonymous-message tool on top of Instagram, from about $10k to 100M+ downloads. He covers shipping fast, simple first-session funnels, riding another platform's graph, user-voice copy, and treating early failures as a portfolio.

chunks.heading: How Hunter builds simple, fast consumer apps: the NGL playbook
chunks.text:
Hunter J. Isaacson is a 24-year-old app builder. By his account he has built about 10 apps with roughly 150 million downloads and around 30 million dollars in revenue across them. NGL is his biggest. He puts his personal take-home at roughly 2 to 2.5 million dollars by the end of 2024, because he has partners.

His path:
- He earned 70k at his first design job and 100k at his second, plus some consulting, so he was at about 100-120k a year before NGL.
- He started college at USC's Marshall business school but never intended to graduate.
- He spent his first two and a half years failing. His first product was a Gen Z take on Foursquare (check in, pickup points, leaderboards), built with outsourced developers he managed poorly.
- He says the failure was the most important stage. In his view, people who skip failing are the ones who get delayed.

chunks.heading: Fail, then build a portfolio of attempts
chunks.text:
- Hunter calls his failures "your portfolio." He likes seeing entrepreneurs with many projects listed, because it shows they aren't scared to try and are iterating.
- NGL was roughly his eighth app. He says very few people (he names Evan Spiegel and Mark Zuckerberg) hit with their first.
- He never launches something and sees it succeed the next week. His method is to launch, test-market, and spend time iterating.
- He argues that quitting too early is the common mistake. NGL got almost no traffic for its first four months.
- His turning point was cold-DMing an Instagram contact one year older who had already sold an app. They had lunch in 2020, and the contact told him "everything you're doing is wrong." Hunter pivoted and says the advice was real and raw.

chunks.heading: Make people comfortable, and keep apps simple
chunks.text:
- Zoom University (2020) was a two-on-two video chat app for college students: two guys and two girls in a four-way call. It reached about 200k downloads and had a 7 to 1 girl-to-guy ratio, which is unheard of in dating. His explanation is that everyone brings a friend, so everyone feels comfortable.
- His lesson: be a safe place for users.
- At Wink (a make-new-friends app he designed at a company that hired him at 21, now around 30 million downloads), he learned that refining existing features beats adding more.
- His rule: build a very core MVP in six to eight weeks, launch it, and iterate quickly.
- Wink also taught him platform leverage. Locked features could be unlocked with in-app currency, and users earned that currency for free by posting on Snapchat.

chunks.heading: NGL: a tool that piggybacks on Instagram
chunks.text:
- What it does: you enter your Instagram username and get a link to post on your story. Others tap it and send an anonymous message, which passes through two layers of AI moderation for bullying and harassment. You then reply publicly on Instagram.
- His framing: "build tools not networks." It is the Instagram Q&A feature made anonymous, which gets more, funnier and more dramatic responses. Influencers use it for that reason.
- He says the app game is making 20-30% improvements on existing products and marketing them in a unique way, noting Meta cloned Twitter.
- The launch timing was right after Instagram opened links to everyone.
- The first version was bare bones.
- Over four months of "crickets," the team renamed the company, reworked the branding, design, flow and funnel, and ran UGC and influencer link tests.
- The company was bootstrapped with about 10k, of which 4k went to a domain they never used.
- They built Android once they saw signs of growth. Hunter says if you see growth you must build both platforms immediately, though starting iOS-only is fine.

chunks.heading: The breakout and the numbers
chunks.text:
- One UGC TikTok did about 1 million views in a day, mostly in Europe, the Middle East, North Africa and South America. It showed a girl getting a dramatic anonymous message.
- Downloads went from a first 1,000 in a day to 1.5 million in a day within a week.
- At peak they did about 990,000 downloads per hour, and metrics providers kept shutting them off for exceeding rate limits.
- Revenue peaked at tens of thousands of dollars a minute.
- Results: 100+ million downloads, number one in 150+ countries, and the most downloaded app in the world in summer 2023. It now sits around the top 25 in the US.
- His rank strategy: pop to number one hard, then hold in the top 50.
- The app is translated into every language Apple supports. Most downloads are overseas, and they localized in about 90 days.

chunks.heading: Speed to the magic moment
chunks.text:
- His one-word answer on what mattered most: speed. "Teams that ship fast win."
- He says to build for the "lizard brain": very simple products.
- Session one matters, not day one. Users must reach the aha moment within minutes (NGL's was about 60 seconds), or they fall out of the funnel.
- The first-time experience should be a guided sandbox, as TikTok's first scroll and Tinder's fifth swipe are.
- Any product needs a clear expectation, a simple action, and an obvious reward. The reward is someone else's expectation: people see replies on your story, so they tap the link.
- His aim is to create a social movement, not just an app. Friends posted NGL on every story for months.

chunks.heading: Talk like your users
chunks.text:
- He applies this to any consumer product: be memeable and funny, as Liquid Death and the Slim Jim Twitter account are.
- NGL's Instagram has over a million organic followers. It posts memes and the funniest messages sent through the app. He ran it first, then hired a social media manager.
- Specifics:
  - App copy says "IG," not Instagram.
  - Things are lowercase where possible.
  - Notifications are written like a user would text, such as "your inbox is dry" with a cactus emoji, or "flooded" with a wet emoji.
- Example: his dad called to say the deli cashier had just received an NGL notification.
- He estimates this was worth millions.

chunks.heading: Community as a movement
chunks.text:
- His undisclosed-until-now tip: make people feel part of a big movement by engaging them directly.
- During the growth spurt, he and his co-founders hand-replied to every Instagram DM for months, hyped up users, and reposted users' praise to a large account.
- NGL's website has a "love wall" of 100+ DMs.
- He says users became evangelists, and the effect was bigger than he expected.

chunks.heading: Finding opportunities and what's next
chunks.text:
- App revenue and download data is public. He says you can browse App Store rankings by category and find apps doing about 50k downloads a month and 250k in cash.
- Exit options for a successful app: another big app or private equity.
- His next focus is apps where each user is worth more, either monetized more or with more valuable user information, rather than chasing 100 million downloads at a low monetization rate. He says NGL has a ceiling and wants one with a higher ceiling.

chunks.heading: Advice for beginners
chunks.text:
- Pick one skill (design, engineering, marketing, copywriting, editing, videography) and get good at it. Money follows.
- His dad's rule: don't chase money, chase passion, but pick a passion where people can make money.
- Build a team from your network. Other 17-18 year olds are hustling and will become co-founders.
- Make your own mistakes rather than copying his.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hunter J. Isaacson, a designer turned serial app founder, explains how NGL hit 250M downloads with zero paid marketing. He covers proving a viral loop in a small friend graph, one-step onboarding, one-action screens, GDP-based pricing, and equity structure.

chunks.heading: How Hunter finds app ideas and validates them
chunks.text:
- Hunter picks ideas based on whether the mechanic can go viral on its own, not on formal validation. In his words, "It was all intuition with the assumption it has to be viral."
- His key lesson came from Wink, his earlier friend-making app. Users got 100 free gems and each right swipe cost 10 gems. After 10 swipes a popup offered two options: buy gems for 99 cents or share on Snapchat. That share-or-pay gate produced millions of organic downloads, and it showed him that you can use other platforms to grow a new app.
- When Instagram opened link stickers to everyone in October 2021, he applied that lesson. He built NGL, an anonymous Q&A app, in 3-4 weeks.
- He builds eight apps before the big hit. His first app (a Gen Z Foursquare) died when COVID hit. His second, Zoom University (a live video college double-dating app, built in 2020), reached a couple hundred thousand downloads and top 10 in social. That was the first time he felt "this is possible."
- Wink reached roughly 60-70 million downloads.
- He says the earlier you start, the better. You need to fail and "crawl through the mud" before the money comes.

chunks.heading: How NGL went viral: the loop and the small-scale proof
chunks.text:
- NGL launched in late 2021 with almost no traction for about 6 months. Nobody cloned it in that time.
- The viral loop works like this:
  - A user's first exposure is a friend posting the link on their story. That works as social proof, because young people do what their friends do.
  - They tap the link and send an anonymous message.
  - A big button after sending says to get your own messages, so they download the app.
  - They already know what the receiving side feels like, so posting their own link feels safe.
- Replies matter more than links. Friends who see a link with no replies leave. Once they see replies on the story, they realize others are sending messages and it's socially acceptable. The "perfect user" posts a link and shares a few replies.
- The core principle: prove the product at small scale first. If you can get one school or one friend graph to adopt it, it will spread globally. The hard part is reaching that tipping point.
- Hunter defines the friend graph as the people you know and the mutual friends you share. The goal is to get everyone in one friend graph posting so their friends see it and it spreads.
- He also tested activating random high schools one by one before it went viral, though it didn't always work.

chunks.heading: The break: New Zealand, Android and 5-10 TikToks
chunks.text:
