- In April-May 2022, NGL popped off in New Zealand and Australia. The trigger was an influencer paid about $50 to post the link. One of her followers was popular in high school, posted it, and that activated the whole school.
- Growth stalled there. Hunter was watching Firebase graphs and saw usage bouncing between New Zealand and Australia without spreading. He realized the region was Android-heavy and NGL had no Android app.
- He called a friend, asked how fast an Android app could be built, and got three weeks. Hunter admits he was in an "iOS bubble."
- After launching Android, the team pushed about 5-10 TikToks. One got 1 million views. After that they never paid for marketing again.
- Results:
  - Downloads went from about 1,000 a day to about 1.5 million in a day within days (about 90,000 an hour).
  - The target to hit was roughly 1,000 users in one day, at which point the story permeated the whole friend graph.
  - Total: 250 million downloads, zero marketing spend after that, 100% organic.
- Total marketing spend before the break was roughly $5-7K of testing, with about $10K in total expenses (including a few thousand on a domain they never used).
- A funny detail: the viral TikTok creator was on a CPM deal, and the video hit 1 million views, which meant they owed about $3K they didn't have. His co-founder suggested taking it down. They did, and it didn't matter because it had already activated. They later paid her much more.
- He says NGL was built by design for this: they proved critical mass in one region, then fixed what blocked scaling.

chunks.heading: Onboarding and product psychology rules
chunks.text:
- NGL onboarding during the viral period was one step: type your Instagram username. No login, no authentication, no phone number. It only pulled the profile picture to put on the story asset.
- After signup the app gives a link with a 3-4 step tutorial: copy the link, share it. At the time links couldn't be auto-attached to stories, so the team effectively trained a quarter of a billion people to use Instagram's link feature.
- Replies are shared to the user's story from a big share button in the inbox, and the question posts anonymously.
- His design rules:
  - **One central action per page.** There is always a big obvious button, because young people are easily distracted and doubt makes them leave for TikTok.
  - **One main onboarding flow** with no branching, running straight to the core metric. For NGL that meant getting someone to share a link and a few replies as fast as possible.
  - **Make the main button pulse, glow or wiggle.** He calls this the last 5% of polish most people skip, and says it is what gets people to finish.
  - **Make products work the way people assume they should.** Meeting expectations makes a product feel great; missing them makes it feel bad (his example: a bad coffee in a paper cup at a nice shop).
  - **Ask where the user's eyes go first** and what a human would do on each screen. Apply this across the whole app, not only onboarding.
  - **Use anticipation moments for loading time.** Tell users something is being prepared ("ETA one minute"), then deliver it faster than expected, ideally with confetti. He calls this framing and priming.
- Colors: NGL is red, orange and yellow. He picked them because Instagram's icon is pink and orange and he wanted NGL to look good next to it. He adds that people tap red buttons.
- Name: it started as Ask.fun. He came up with "NGL" on his own in spring 2022, before it went viral, because it is culturally relevant to the demographic and explains itself ("my NGL link", "I'm not going to lie, I'll send anonymous messages").

chunks.heading: NGL monetization and global pricing
chunks.text:
- Revenue is from weekly subscriptions in every country.
- Pricing is localized by the GDP of each country. Examples he gives: roughly $1 a week in smaller or lower-income markets versus around $5-8 a week in the US. His reasoning is that $10 a week is a salary in some countries and he didn't want to price out parts of the world.
- The app is also translated into every language, and he credits this localization for global growth, with large usage in Asia, the Middle East and North Africa.
- Premium features are hints about who sent a message (location, phone type and similar factors, which kids use to guess who it was) and seeing viewers of your link. He says nobody got upset about the premium features.
- NGL is now close to an optimized version of what it was. It does about 100 million downloads a year, still with no marketing. Hunter says people who churn often return because the viral loop keeps looping and a friend posts a link. It is passive cash flow, so he hasn't sold it. It's about two and a half years into significant revenue, run by his co-founders on autopilot.
- Hunter has never done paid advertising, so he says he is not the expert, though he is open to it for Bags.

chunks.heading: Scaling pains after going viral
chunks.text:
- When the app blew up, everything broke. Software providers shut them off, API usage hit billions of requests, and bills piled up on every platform.
- They didn't know how long the viral wave would last, so they didn't know how much to spend on software providers.
- Apple pays out on a delay (he says about 60 days), so cash was tight. He and his co-founders had to take a loan to cover software bills. The first 3-6 months were hard before it calmed down.
- He also dealt with odd requests, including emails from international police forces and military, and users DMing the team just to get attention.
- On the App Store, he calls it a "pure meritocracy" because everyone builds with the same tools and compute. His one tip is to not submit until the app is mostly ready, since review feedback will force fixes and long review cycles get annoying.

chunks.heading: Team, process and tools for building apps
chunks.text:
- Team recipe: a product/design lead, an engineer (a technical lead or CTO), and a growth person who handles influencer outreach and videos. One person can cover more than one role.
- Hunter splits equity far more evenly than most founders. His reasoning: people have to wake up at 3 a.m. when things crash, and they need meaningful equity to do that. Good engineers are hard to find.
- Simple-app timeline: about a week of design in Figma, then engineers scope and break it into tasks and build module by module. Hunter then gets a build and tries to break it, creates a QA list, sends it to developers, and repeats a few rounds before launch. Complex apps (photo, video) take longer.
- Stack he lists: Figma, App Store Connect, TestFlight, Firebase or AWS, an AI coding environment such as Cursor, Xcode, and Mixpanel or Amplitude for analytics. NGL is built in Swift, which he likes for access to the full phone and smooth animation. Bags uses React Native, cross-platform.
- He started as a designer, then moved to product lead and founder. He does his own branding, color, interfaces, navigation, copy and vibe. He says he built eight years of apps and calls Figma speed his edge.
- His first job was the only designer at a mobile app holding company, where his mentor (the CEO) had him study existing apps. The team printed screens and put them on the office whiteboard. He treats the two years there as his college.

chunks.heading: Bags: building a consumer crypto trading app
chunks.text:
- Bags is a social crypto trading app (a DEX on Solana) launched in November 2024. Hunter bootstrapped it with money from NGL, started ideating in summer 2023 and went fully locked in from the start of 2024.
- His bet is that "the real battle of crypto is going to be fought on the app store" and that crypto will go mobile and social.
- Product:
  - Sign up in about 5 seconds with email or other login, build a profile in seconds, fund the wallet with Apple Pay, and buy a memecoin within 60 seconds.
  - The app looks more like a credit card wallet than a crypto wallet. It uses an embedded, non-custodial wallet whose keys can be exported.
  - Users can follow friends and see what they traded, check leaderboards, join group chats, and see a "bags for you" feed.
  - It includes live charts and data with filters.
- Economics: Bags takes a standard 1% fee on buys and sells, with no fees on sending or receiving. The majority of fees are passed back to active traders and to people whose followers trade. Everyone has an auto referral link and earns a percentage of fees from people they refer. Group chats also act as ref links.
- Early traction: over 300,000 registered profiles (fewer active traders). The key finding is that users who fund their card have high retention and high session time. The main goal now is getting people to fund their account and reach the first trade and profit-locking moment faster.
- Order of operations: the team spent the months after launch on performance (landing 99.9% of transactions in a couple of seconds), plus a new auth system, because early sign-in required Twitter. Getting the best data feeds is what gets users the best price. Marketing started only after enough bugs were fixed.
- Growth plan: level one is UGC and short videos aimed at finance people and crypto-curious users who see memecoin profits on TikTok and Instagram. He wants to build the foundation first and layer growth features after, and says he is more open to paid ads for Bags than for NGL.

chunks.heading: Studios, selling and long-term bets
chunks.text:
- Hunter says the app studio model works if you want to throw many products at the wall, find one that hits, then double down on it.
- He chose not to run a studio for Bags because he knew the problem and the market he loved, even if he didn't know the exact product.
- He prefers a longer-term business that evolves with him over a quick build-and-sell, and he didn't sell NGL because it still cash flows.
- He thinks ICOs and app tokens may eventually replace IPOs for modern consumer tech companies, though it could take around 20 years and he has made no formal token announcement for Bags.
- He credits Steve Jobs, Brian Chesky (and the Stanford Blitzscaling podcast), Evan Spiegel and Walter Isaacson's Elon Musk biography as product-focused influences. The most impactful book he names is Reality Transurfing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hunter Isaacson, co-founder of NGL and Bags (300M+ downloads across his apps), explains how he designs viral loops, onboarding and first-session experiences. He also covers launching with just the loop, spotting existing behavior to build on, and designing a lifestyle first. The back half drifts into worldview talk (humanoid robots, ancient tech, consciousness).

chunks.heading: Hunter's route to building apps: design-first, MVP-light
chunks.text:
- Hunter started his first app at 18, in a 3-month gap before USC, expecting a billion-dollar company in a year. He learned it was much harder but loved the process.
- He is technical on web and product (modded Minecraft servers at 12-13) but hires strong engineers for apps. His own skill is design and product. He "became known as the guy" for app design in his builder group, which brought partnership invitations.
- His career path: Zoom University (a college double-dating video app, roughly a quarter million downloads or fewer), then Wink (a make-new-friends app, 70M+ downloads, where he was an employee and designer, not an owner), then NGL as his eighth app. He says NGL took many failures to reach.
- At about 21 he was recruited by the former president of Musical.ly (which became TikTok). He spent almost two years there as the only designer, building half a dozen apps while the company grew from 12 to 50-60 people. He calls it a lab where he could test many hypotheses.
- He built NGL in about four weeks from idea to launch, then saw six months of nobody using it before product-market fit.

chunks.heading: Lessons from his mentor: session one and A/B testing
chunks.text:
- Focus on "session one" rather than D1/D7/D30 retention. The goal is to get the user to do something meaningful in the first session, so that even if they close the app you got something.
- Make onboarding flawless, aiming for 99% of people to complete it.
- Test relentlessly. He cared more about UI than UX early on and learned "it's not about making an art project". A good-looking purple gradient button can lose to a red one on conversion.
- Colors that win in his apps: red, blue, green. He writes all of the copy himself so the tone stays consistent.
- Ask what problem each screen solves, not whether it looks good.

chunks.heading: The viral loop playbook (NGL)
chunks.text:
- NGL spread because your friend's Instagram story post is both the discovery channel and a "stamp of approval". Seeing multiple friends post it creates social safety ("this is normal, not weird").
- Onboarding takes 1-2 steps with no auth, 15-20 seconds. The user has their link posted within about 60 seconds of download.
- Having sent a message to a friend's link, the new user already knows what receiving feels like, so the value is proven before the install. That loop is why growth kept going (over 250M downloads since June 2022, not slowing).
- NGL had no marketing budget. It unlocked Instagram as a channel because link-in-story only became available around the end of 2021.
- Instagram follow button: NGL has over 2M followers because the app has a "follow us" button. The page works as a legitimacy stamp and a retention nudge.
- Per-app comparison: Wink's session one was a swipe stack with 100 gems, minus 10 per right swipe. At the end a pop-up offered premium or "share on your story for free", which taught him people share a lot when asked at the right moment.

chunks.heading: Hunter's framework for a new app
chunks.text:
1. Pick a name everyone understands and can pronounce, that works in every language (NGL = "not gonna lie"; Bags = money bags).
2. Design young and fun, with clean copy.
3. Decide what you need in onboarding (phone, email, birthday, gender, or nothing).
4. Define session one right after onboarding (NGL: copy link, share, get messages, reply on story).
5. Create an aha moment fast, then immediately ask for a share or direct invite, in context (a dating app is better asking users to text a best friend than to post on a story).
6. Pick one North Star metric (NGL: link shares and replies; Bags: users who fund their accounts).
7. Don't overbuild. Crush onboarding and session one, then add a little more.

He says to find behavior that already exists, unoptimized, on the internet or other apps. Bags came from users already trading meme coins across disconnected wallet, screener, exchange and messenger apps. NGL came from the Ask.fm-style anonymous format on a new channel.

chunks.heading: Bags: launch with the viral loop before the product
chunks.text:
- Bags is a financial app to buy and sell crypto with Apple Pay, aiming to be the simplest way for anyone to buy crypto, then pay with it. He has been in crypto since 2017.
- Launch order: the first release had only claimable Bags links (every profile link is a wallet), with no wallets yet. People shared their links, tapped through to a site, claimed theirs and shared again, the same loop as NGL.
- That produced a couple hundred thousand registered profiles and over 100,000 Twitter followers. He says that is a lot for crypto and "nothing" for his other apps.
- His reasoning: acceptable user counts depend on average revenue per user. A financial app with money in it has higher ARPU and retention than a social app, so it needs fewer users. He notes most NGL users never monetized.
- Bags took 6+ months to build, with a rebuild and core feature changes. Security is handled by large external providers, with multiple login methods and authenticator-app 2FA.
- His advice: once you have a basic MVP, go on TikTok and "start pumping videos". If it works you will know.

chunks.heading: Lifestyle design and manifestation
chunks.text:
- At 15 he manifested a luxury lifestyle: a fake version of a luxury watch, styled clothes, visits to Lamborghini dealerships at 17. Years later he realized he was living what he had told himself.
- His advice: "design your lifestyle before you do anything." Think 10-30 years ahead (where you live, kids, career, friendships, daily routine). Work backwards to the industries that deliver that lifestyle, then your unique edge, then pick a skill (his was design).
- Passion should be able to make money: "do not chase money, chase your passion", but check that the passion supports the lifestyle you want.
- Radical self-accountability: treat everything in your life as your doing. Each month he notes his biggest problem on his phone, and when it is solved he rereads it as a reminder.

chunks.heading: Questioning everything and being early
chunks.text:
- Hunter says his money came after he started questioning things. His mind opened from 2018 and widened by 2020, after he noticed false claims in the news and asked what else was untrue.
- His self-described edge: "I'm usually just early." Looking at an issue from every angle and not following man-made protocols gives you the conviction to build early. He says this is common sense.
- His practice: doubt everything, including his own claims, in the sense of seeking truth. Debates with friends are to find the answer, not to be right.
- He believes the world is in a transition between old and new systems, expecting humanoid robots in homes in about 10-15 years with significant adoption, and says AI will free human time. He is concerned it could go toward tyranny instead of abundance.
- He holds speculative views (ancient advanced civilizations, hidden land, free energy) that are his opinions and not business guidance.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hunter J. Isaacson explains how he went from failed apps to co-founding NGL (150M MAU) with about $5,000 and no venture funding. He covers picking ideas by psychological driver, designing viral loops where users market for you, using UGC only to seed the first users, monetizing without breaking the core promise, and why he avoided raising.

chunks.heading: Building apps from failures: Hunter's path to NGL
chunks.text:
- Hunter's first company, started at 18, raised about $150,000 from friends and family. He spent roughly 2.5 years building a gamified-life app (go to a location, capture a photo or video, stitched into a reel). It never left TestFlight, and COVID killed it.
- After that failure he dropped his founder ego and worked as a product designer, building a reputation. He shipped Zoom University (about 250,000 downloads), a college-ID-gated video-chat dating app.
- By his account, NGL was his eighth app, and the first that made him serious money. Earlier apps got downloads, but he didn't control the company, so he earned less.
- His view on how skill develops: "You acquire it through getting [expletive] on by the market." You only know a product journey works after five other versions failed.
- He built five or six apps in one year as the sole designer, handling every screen and QA pass himself.
- He scaled one earlier app to about half a million daily active users. He watched feature additions make the numbers go down, which taught him users don't know what they want.
- His rule: find the drop-off point in the numbers first. Don't build ten features to fill a hole. Usually a tiny adjustment is needed, not a new feature set.
- Simple products are often what the customer wants, even when developers mock them for it.
- Earlier work: Wink, a make-friends/dating app, did about 70 million downloads across 2020-2021.

chunks.heading: Picking an idea: existing behavior, Maslow, and a clean lane
chunks.text:
- Hunter looks for behavior users already do that is unoptimized, then offers a faster flow and a better experience.
- Signal to watch: several apps blowing up in a category but not really hitting. Ask why you haven't seen the winning app yet. Usually users aren't sharing, the design is weak, or the marketing is off.
- He wants a noticeable product improvement plus a brand improvement. Brand matters: ask.fm got little use, but renamed NGL ("not gonna lie") it signaled anonymous and cool immediately.
- He looks for a niche or channel competitors aren't pursuing. Nobody had built an anonymous-messaging app for Instagram, so it was a "clean lane."
- Filter: if an idea doesn't hit a level of Maslow's hierarchy (love and acceptance, what friends think of me, purpose, money), he won't build it.
- The test: the psychological driver for sharing must be strong. If he can't figure out why user A would bring user B, he drops it. He says he has many half-baked ideas shelved for this reason.
- Empathy and brand context matter: "curate an empathetic experience" (a phrase from his friend Sam). Know exactly who you're building for.
- Naming examples: Wink (winking at someone, friend or date), NGL (anonymous feedback), Bags (what crypto people call their holdings).

chunks.heading: How NGL was conceived and built
chunks.text:
- Instagram opened link sharing to everyone in October 2021; before that you needed 10,000 followers.
- Within 7 days his friend Isaiah Turner called with the idea: an anonymous messaging app. The group of consumer social builders had been obsessing over what to build with link sharing.
- NGL: post a link to your Instagram story, people tap it and send anonymous messages, you reply on your story. It's an anonymous version of the Instagram question sticker.
- It took about 3-4 weeks to build. Nothing existed for Instagram then, though older anonymous apps existed on other platforms.
- Then about 6 months of "crickets." The team worked on getting 95%+ of new users to post the link, and to share multiple replies, within about 60 seconds.
- Posting the link was a five-step manual process then (tap sticker, paste link, position it). They rewrote the explainer screens until it worked.
- NGL was built with about $5,000. He says it has generated "tens and tens and tens of millions" since.
- Scale cited: biggest app in the world by summer 2022; 150 million monthly active users and over 250 million downloads.
- Hunter said he has never raised venture as an entrepreneur.

chunks.heading: The viral loop: sender first, then receiver
chunks.text:
- His core model: UGC gets the first users in, and a loop turns them into more users. Without a loop, founders keep spending on UGC, hit hard paywalls, watch everyone drop off, and reset the next month.
- Highest-signal endorsement is a friend inviting you or posting publicly. Design for "How do I get you to post it?"
- The loop must not make users look lame: "You want a viral loop that doesn't make you look lame... It makes you look socially acceptable."
- NGL's loop: your first experience is as the sender, not the receiver. You see a friend's link, send them a message, and see them reply on their story.
- After sending, a large pulsing button says "Get your own messages." You've just done the thing your friend benefits from, so you want that benefit yourself.
- Result: downloads became "free." Everyone who writes a message wants to post their own link, and the loop still drives the app 3.5+ years later.
- Activation testing: spend about $100-$200 to get an influencer to post the link, then manually watch every public story to see where users failed (forgot the link, misplaced it). Iterate in batches of a few hundred downloads until everyone understood the steps.
- Advice he echoed: if an app idea has no built-in spread mechanism, it may not be worth pursuing.

chunks.heading: UGC strategy and how NGL took off
chunks.text:
- UGC means user-generated content, an actual user making content instead of a big, expensive influencer.
- In 2020 he and friends used a "fresh account" strategy. They hired TikTokers with under 50,000 followers at CPMs of $3 or less. They also ran VPN tactics, posting across For You pages. He calls this the "Wild West era."
- Now it is more regulated and commercialized, with professional UGC creators. Back then roughly 1 in 10 videos hit a million views; now it's closer to 1 in 100-500.
- Pre-launch NGL's UGC test was only 5-10 videos with scripts he wrote, at an agreed $3 CPM. Within 48 hours one video hit a million views, then 1,000 users became 10,000, and within about 36 hours it reached 1.5 million users.
- His use of UGC: get 1,000-10,000 users, then let the loop do the rest. He didn't rely on UGC to reach hundreds of millions of downloads.
- Platforms now distribute on video merit rather than follower count, so a creator with 1,000 followers can still get hundreds of thousands of views.

chunks.heading: Monetizing NGL and early financing
chunks.text:
- Thesis: if NGL went viral (5-10 million downloads), carving out 1-2% of users into a pro subscription would make money.
- Desire he targeted: everyone wants to know who sent the message. NGL stays anonymous, so the paid feature is "hints," a pseudo-anonymous reveal.
- Hints use identifiers such as phone type, location, area code, carrier, and whether the sender has messaged before. This served power users without breaking the anonymity promise.
- Growing pains: a six-figure Mixpanel bill after about two days of data; he swapped analytics platforms constantly to dodge bills.
- Apple payouts are delayed: money made in January arrives in March. He was personally broke while the app made money.
- The only financing was a bridge loan from services that look at App Store MRR, for about 60 days. NGL had seven-figure MRR; the amount was roughly $100-$200K.
- Tools: Firebase for simpler apps like NGL (dashboard, databases, hot swapping); more complex apps like Bags didn't use it. Amplitude or Mixpanel for analytics, depending on his CTO's preference. Slack and App Store Connect.

chunks.heading: Why he avoids venture funding
chunks.text:
- Belief: "You only understand the value of money when you have it." He has seen founders raise $25 million, lose their minds, and burn the company.
- He wants to have respect for money before raising. He doesn't rule out raising someday.
- Consumer apps: "you need two devs and a designer and then that's it." Funding is unnecessary unless the concept is capital-intensive, like rockets.
- He did help venture-backed companies, and raised venture at a company he worked at when he was 21-22, but never as an entrepreneur.

chunks.heading: Bags: crypto, meme coins, and royalties
chunks.text:
- Background: bought his first Bitcoin around May 2017 (about $1,500), watched it hit $20,000, then crashed and got hacked. He kept building apps through 2018-2021, tried NFTs in 2021 without success, and got into crypto heavily around 2022-2023.
- He wanted to build a crypto app in 2017 after finding Coinbase poor. After NGL crossed 100 million users, he moved to it.
- Bags context (2023): no real mobile trading apps; trading was on web and Telegram bots. He and co-founder Finn (who left D Gods) wanted to bring crypto to mobile.
- Early product: a beta app with a large group chat and native in-chat trading. They sold an OG membership to about 35,000 people to seed evangelists. Then came a full trading app and a launchpad.
- Meme coin thesis: communities want skin in the game, and a holder identifies with others holding the same asset. Early idea: holder group chats, treating holdings as a social graph.
- Core product bet: meme coins lacked a revenue-generating business model. Bags built royalties into coins so projects earn from fees, reinvest them, split them, or pay dividends. He calls Bags the best way for meme coins to launch and make sustainable revenue.
- Team shout-outs: Finn, CTO Ramo, Dan.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hunter Isaacson, founder of NGL and Bags, talks about moving from a viral social app to a crypto banking app. He covers bias to action, not repeating your first win, building what you personally need, and treating each exit as the next round. Much of the rest is spiritual and futurist speculation.

chunks.heading: Building NGL and why he stopped competing with himself
chunks.text:
- Hunter built his first company at 17-18. He failed for a while, made no money and was "dirt poor", then slowly had apps start to work. He went from failed entrepreneur to employee, then realized he was an entrepreneur after all.
- He says he learned he "could just do things" when NGL blew up: it hit millions of downloads a day.
- NGL is an anonymous-questions app where friends ask each other questions and post the answers to their Instagram stories. It has about 250 million users and, by his figures, does $100 million a year.
- He also cites Wink at 70 million downloads.
- His first app idea, "Rally", came in 2015 when he was 18. It was a Tinder-style party app where a host sets up a party and approves who can attend, replacing messy Facebook invite lists. He had a dev build an MVP, then dropped it.
- He says it matched Partiful "feature for feature". His takeaway is that ideas float in the ether and you can pick one up when you are tuned in.

chunks.heading: Why he left social apps for finance (Bags)
chunks.text:
- After NGL he had many social-app ideas ready to go, each reusing the same social dynamics. He decided not to build another social app aimed at 500 million users.
- His reasoning: "sometimes in life you have to not compete with your former self." Founders repeat their first win and deliberately re-make themselves the underdog in the same space. He had already hit that level.
- He moved to consumer finance and crypto, a space he had loved for years, around 2023. He wanted to bank the underbanked, debanked and unbanked, and move people away from centralized banking.
- He built it partly for himself, because he feared being debanked. During COVID he was censored online for his views, and several tech friends were debanked.
- NGL pushed free speech (anonymous, with only bullying filters). Bags pushes personal freedom and sovereignty: "your money should be yours."
- The vision: bring a billion people into crypto and change how money moves. He wants Bags to be the app people think of for anything financial: making money, organizing and spending it, and talking about it with friends.
- He is asset-agnostic. Memecoins are today's use case, but "crypto is cyclical", so Bags will support whatever the asset class becomes.

chunks.heading: What building in crypto actually takes
chunks.text:
- Hunter says building in crypto is the opposite of investing in it: "Building in crypto requires years. Investing in crypto requires minutes."
- Good devs are hard to find, especially mobile devs who also understand crypto.
- APIs are limited and documentation is thin, so you build much from scratch.
- Many infrastructure providers don't scale.
- Even basics like landing a transaction or pulling data from the chain are harder than they sound.
- His view is that crypto is only now at the point where people can build in it, and it is still hard.

chunks.heading: Money, wins and staying a builder
chunks.text:
- He argues you are in the same position whether rich or broke: you are still building. Friends who went from millionaire to nothing in crypto found it "not that different"; only their egos were hurt.
- His analogy is Monopoly. Each win is passing Go and collecting $200, and then you see another level: "There's just more hotels on the board."
- He says that to be free in today's system you need billions, and he calls money "slavery in a sense."
- He expects transacting to persist in some form, such as goods or AI compute, but not as paper dollars. That is why he thinks consumer finance will always have a role.

chunks.heading: His view of AI, robots and the economy
chunks.text:
- He thinks the real iPhone replacement is the humanoid robot, with glasses and contacts as companions. His comparison: 15 years ago a boarding pass on your phone was wild, and now it is normal.
- He expects a society of abundance, with robots building 24/7. Much human capital is wasted today on people working jobs they hate.
- He predicts the new status metric for wealthy people will be how many robots they own, not how many jets.
- He expects money to change radically because it represents scarcity, and abundance removes scarcity. He thinks it moves toward peer-to-peer, sovereign communities and city-states rather than large nations and central banks.
- He expects school in its current form to disappear and be replaced by something like apprenticeship. He says the best part of school is social development, such as learning to handle bullies and peer pressure.
- He expects a split in society: some go fully into the metaverse, while others keep the technology but go spiritual and build with old techniques.
- His darker thesis is a long war with AI, with robots fighting robots, tiny weaponized drones and engineered viruses. He says people will have to rediscover ancient frequency and sound technology, and he plans to leave cities for a protected island.

- On Kanye, Hunter says some people's role in society is to push the Overton window, so that what they said years ago becomes acceptable. He respects Kanye as probably the best artist of the last 30 years.
